title: Keys and Constraints
summary: A constraint is a rule that a database checks when data is added or changed.
introduction: A constraint is a rule that a database checks when data is added or changed. A school list should not have two students with the same id. Use rules to protect ids, required values and links between tables.
learningObjectives: Choose primary keys, including composite keys
Enforce UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK and DEFAULT rules
Link tables with FOREIGN KEY and choose an ON DELETE action
Enable foreign key enforcement in SQLite

blocks.text: You could validate data in application code, but there is usually more than one application, plus scripts, imports and manual fixes. A constraint lives with the table, so it applies to all of them. When a statement would break a rule, the database rejects it with an error and leaves the data unchanged.

A **primary key** uniquely identifies each row; it is automatically `NOT NULL` and `UNIQUE`, and other tables refer to it. Most tables use a surrogate integer id. When a combination of columns is naturally unique, a **composite key** lists them together, which also prevents duplicate pairs:

blocks.content:
OK: CREATE TABLE enrollments (
OK: INSERT INTO enrollments VALUES (1, 10), (1, 11), (2, 10)
UNIQUE constraint failed: enrollments.student_id, enrollments.course_id — in: INSERT INTO enrollments VALUES (1, 10)

blocks.text: The error names both key columns. Note the pattern: the first three rows were inserted, the duplicate was rejected, and the playground stopped at the error.
UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK and DEFAULT

rows: No two rows share the value
The condition must be true for every row
Used when the insert omits the column

blocks.content:
OK: CREATE TABLE accounts (
OK: INSERT INTO accounts (email, balance) VALUES ('ada@example.com', 120)
OK: INSERT INTO accounts (email) VALUES ('grace@example.com')

id | email             | balance
---+-------------------+--------
1  | ada@example.com   | 120
2  | grace@example.com | 0

blocks.text: Breaking a rule produces a specific error. The second account below reuses an email address:

blocks.content:
OK: CREATE TABLE accounts (
OK: INSERT INTO accounts (email, balance) VALUES ('ada@example.com', 120)
UNIQUE constraint failed: accounts.email — in: INSERT INTO accounts (email, balance) VALUES ('ada@example.com', 50)

blocks.text: A **foreign key** declares that a column holds values from another table's primary key: `orders.customer_id REFERENCES customers(id)`. The sample `orders` table already carries that declaration. With enforcement on, you cannot insert an order for a customer who does not exist, and you cannot delete a customer who still has orders unless you say what should happen to them.

blocks.title: SQLite ignores foreign keys by default
blocks.text: For backwards compatibility SQLite only enforces `REFERENCES` when the connection runs `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON`. Each playground run is a new connection, so put that line first. PostgreSQL always enforces foreign keys; MySQL does with the InnoDB engine (the default). Forgetting the pragma is the most common reason an SQLite application ends up with orphaned rows.
Without the pragma, an order for the non-existent customer 99 is accepted:

blocks.content:
OK: INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, product_id, quantity, ordered_on)

id | customer_id
---+------------
9  | 99

blocks.text: With it, the same insert fails:

blocks.content:
OK: PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON
FOREIGN KEY constraint failed — in: INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, product_id, quantity, ordered_on)

blocks.text: The `REFERENCES` clause can say what happens to child rows when the parent is deleted: `RESTRICT` or `NO ACTION` (the default: refuse), `CASCADE` (delete the children too) or `SET NULL` (keep the children, clear the reference). Cascading is right for rows that only make sense with their parent, such as the members of a team:

blocks.content:
OK: PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON
OK: CREATE TABLE teams (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL)
OK: CREATE TABLE members (
OK: INSERT INTO teams (name) VALUES ('Backend'), ('Frontend')
OK: INSERT INTO members (team_id, name) VALUES (1, 'Ada'), (1, 'Linus'), (2, 'Grace'
OK: DELETE FROM teams WHERE id = 1

id | team_id | name
---+---------+------
3  | 2       | Grace

blocks.text: Deleting the Backend team removed Ada and Linus automatically; only Grace from Frontend remains.

Constraints can be named (`CONSTRAINT uq_accounts_email UNIQUE (email)`) so that error messages and `ALTER TABLE ... DROP CONSTRAINT` can refer to them in PostgreSQL and MySQL. SQLite cannot add or drop constraints on an existing table: you create a new table with the desired rules, copy the rows with `INSERT ... SELECT`, drop the old table and rename the new one.

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.text: Insert a second cart item with quantity 0 to see the CHECK error, then one with product id 42 to see the foreign key error.

blocks.title: Try it yourself

questions.question: Which constraint stops two customers from registering the same email address?
questions.explanation: UNIQUE rejects a second row with the same value. NOT NULL only requires a value, CHECK tests a condition on the row itself, and DEFAULT supplies a value when none is given.

questions.question: What does `ON DELETE CASCADE` on `members.team_id` do when a team is deleted?
questions.explanation: CASCADE propagates the delete to the child rows that reference the deleted parent, so the members of that team are removed; other teams are untouched.
options: Deletes the members of that team
Sets the members' team_id to NULL
Deletes every member of every team
